question: What is the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and what should every mobile dev know about it?
answer:
The OWASP Mobile Top 10 names the ten risk categories that most often break real mobile apps, and the 2024 revision is the current one.

• M1 Improper Credential Usage — hardcoded API keys, secrets committed to source.
• M2 Inadequate Supply Chain Security — vulnerable or over-privileged third-party SDKs.
• M3 Insecure Authentication / Authorization — weak token storage, authorization decided on the client.
• M4 Insufficient Input/Output Validation — injection, and XSS inside WebViews.
• M5 Insecure Communication — missing TLS, weak ciphers, no pinning.
• M6 Inadequate Privacy Controls — collecting more PII than declared, no consent gate.
• M7 Insufficient Binary Protections — no obfuscation or integrity checks where the threat model needs them.
• M8 Security Misconfiguration — debug endpoints in production, components left exported.
• M9 Insecure Data Storage — secrets in plain SharedPreferences or UserDefaults. Note that Jetpack Security's `EncryptedSharedPreferences` is deprecated, so new Android code should encrypt with a Keystore-held key itself rather than reaching for that library.
• M10 Insufficient Cryptography — broken algorithms, home-grown constructions, reused nonces.

How to use it: treat it as a review checklist rather than trivia. Thread the categories through code review, run static analysis (MobSF, Detekt security rules, AppSweep), scan dependencies on every bump, and buy a penetration test for anything handling money or health data.

The interview version of this question is usually 'which of these have you actually hit' — having a concrete story about one beats reciting all ten.

question: What does it take to make mobile API traffic hard to intercept and hard to replay?
answer:
No single control protects mobile API traffic, so you layer transport security, token hygiene and server-side attestation on the assumption that every client-side control will eventually be patched out.

• TLS, non-negotiable. Disable cleartext on Android and ship no ATS exceptions on iOS; require TLS 1.2 or better and reject anything older.
• Certificate or SPKI pinning defeats a rogue or user-installed CA. Pin the SPKI hash rather than the leaf certificate, always ship a backup pin, and rotate before expiry — a pinning mistake bricks every installed copy at once and cannot be hotfixed.
• OAuth 2.0 or OIDC with PKCE, in a system browser tab. Never an embedded WebView, never a hand-rolled flow.
• Short-lived access tokens measured in minutes, refresh tokens in Keychain or Keystore, and refresh-token rotation so a stolen one becomes detectable.
• Device and app attestation — Play Integrity on Android, App Attest or DeviceCheck on iOS. It only means something when your server validates the token; a client-side check of the verdict is theatre. Play Integrity's standard request, where you prepare a token provider once and then request per call, is the one to use for anything called often; classic requests are slow and rate-limited.
• Replay protection on endpoints that move money or change credentials: a server-issued nonce plus request signing, with a short validity window.
• Rate limiting and anomaly detection server-side, because that is the one layer an attacker cannot patch.

Say the quiet part out loud in an interview: pinning and obfuscation raise the attacker's cost, they do not stop one. Anything you must genuinely enforce belongs on the server.

question: Client-side root and jailbreak checks can be hooked out in minutes. What do you rely on instead, and what is a client-side check still worth?
answer:
Treat the client's answer as a signal and the server's attestation verdict as the decision — a rooted device can lie about being rooted, so anything enforced only on the client is enforced nowhere.

Server-side attestation, which is what actually holds:
• Play Integrity (Android) returns device labels — `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` for hardware-backed evaluation, and `MEETS_VIRTUAL_INTEGRITY` for emulators — plus separate app and account verdicts. Your backend validates the token and maps the labels to a trust level.
• App Attest and DeviceCheck (iOS) prove the request came from a genuine, unmodified build of your app on real hardware, with a Secure Enclave key bound to that install.

Client-side heuristics, worth having only as an extra signal:
• Android — an `su` binary on the path, BusyBox, Magisk artefacts, test-keys in the build fingerprint, `ro.debuggable` set in a release build. RootBeer bundles the usual set; Magisk's hiding modules defeat most of them.
• iOS — Cydia and apt paths present, writes succeeding outside the sandbox, a registered `cydia` URL scheme handler, unexpected dynamic libraries in the process. IOSSecuritySuite bundles these.
• Both — a debugger attached, or Frida and Objection hooks visible in the process.

On a cross-platform runtime the probe is never yours to make directly:
• Dart, JavaScript and Kotlin/Native see none of these signals — every check is native code reached through a plugin or a channel, so a plugin-free app cannot answer the question at all.
• The resulting boolean lands in a Dart snapshot or a JS bundle, which is cheaper to patch than native code. Ship obfuscated and re-decide server-side.
• Build-mode flags (`kDebugMode`, `__DEV__`) describe your build, not the device, and are not a root check.

What to do with the answer:
• Do not hard-block. Custom ROMs and developer devices are common false positives, and a hard block is the first thing an attacker patches out anyway.
• Degrade by risk instead: refuse to enrol biometrics, force step-up authentication, decline high-value payments, shorten session lifetime.
• Make the decision server-side and send it back as policy the client applies, so the branch an attacker wants to flip is not sitting in the binary.
• Do not name detection functions descriptively and do not tell the user which check fired — that is writing the attacker's changelog for them.

question: Where does a private key actually live on Android and iOS, and how do you guarantee it cannot be extracted?
answer:
The answer to 'where do I put the private key' is 'somewhere you cannot read it either' — both platforms generate the key inside hardware and only ever let you ask it to sign or decrypt.

Android, through the `AndroidKeyStore` provider:
• Generate with `KeyGenParameterSpec`; the key material never enters your process memory.
• StrongBox puts the key in a separate secure element, but throws when the device has no StrongBox, so always catch that and fall back to the TEE-backed key rather than crashing on cheap hardware.
• `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` gates use behind biometrics or the device credential, combined with `BiometricPrompt` and a `CryptoObject`.
• `setAttestationChallenge(...)` yields a certificate chain your server can verify. That is what turns 'I promise this key is hardware-backed' into something checkable.
• Enrolling a new biometric invalidates the key if you asked for that — treat the resulting exception as a re-enrolment trigger, not a crash.

iOS, through the Secure Enclave:
• P-256 keys only, for signing and key agreement. CryptoKit's `SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey` is the readable API; the Keychain equivalent sets `kSecAttrTokenID` to `kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave`.
• `SecAccessControl` binds usage to `.biometryCurrentSet`, which invalidates when Face ID or Touch ID enrolment changes, or to `.userPresence` when you want the passcode to be an acceptable fallback.
• Pick the accessibility class deliberately — the `ThisDeviceOnly` variants stop an item riding a backup onto a different device.

Cross-cutting:
• AES-GCM for symmetric, ECDSA or Ed25519 for signatures, ECDH for agreement, HKDF for derivation. RSA only when a peer forces it, and never a construction of your own design.
• Never reuse a GCM nonce under the same key; store the IV next to the ciphertext.
• Design for rotation on day one: the server accepts several public keys per user during the overlap window, and you re-key on reinstall, on biometric change, and on a failed attestation.

question: How do you keep sensitive content out of screenshots, screen recordings and the clipboard?
answer:
You cannot stop someone photographing the screen, so the goal is narrower: keep secrets out of screenshots, out of the recents thumbnail, out of screen recordings, and out of a clipboard other apps can read.

Screenshots and recording:
• Android — `FLAG_SECURE` on the window blocks screenshots, blanks the surface in recordings, and hides the recents thumbnail. It is per-window, so dialogs and separately presented surfaces need it too.
• Android 14 added a screen-capture callback so you can react to a screenshot instead of only blocking it, and Android 15 added a way to hide just the recents thumbnail without the full `FLAG_SECURE` blackout.
• iOS has no equivalent of `FLAG_SECURE`. You observe the user-took-a-screenshot notification after the fact, watch `UIScreen.isCaptured` while a recording is running, and cover the window with a placeholder as the scene resigns active so the app-switcher snapshot shows nothing.

Clipboard:
• Do not auto-copy secrets. If a one-time code really must be copied, clear it on a timer.
• Android 13 and later — mark the clip with the sensitive-content flag so the system's clipboard preview does not render the value, and the OS clears the clipboard itself after a period. Android also toasts when another app reads the clipboard, so assume every read is observable.
• iOS — set an `expirationDate` on the pasteboard item, and keep it local to the device so it does not travel over Universal Clipboard.

Keyboard and text fields:
• Use the platform's secure input — `SecureTextField` in Compose, `isSecureTextEntry` in UIKit, `SecureField` in SwiftUI. It also excludes the field from recordings.
• Turn off suggestion learning on sensitive fields so secrets never enter the keyboard's personal dictionary.

question: Before an app can ship, what privacy declarations and consent gates does each store require?
answer:
Privacy is a shipping gate now rather than a policy document — both stores reject builds whose declarations do not match what the binary actually does.

Apple:
• App Tracking Transparency — request authorization before any SDK that tracks the user across apps or sites runs, and read the advertising identifier only when the status is authorized. Initialising an ad SDK before the prompt is a rejection, not a warning.
• Privacy nutrition labels in App Store Connect — which data types you collect and whether they are linked to identity.
• Privacy manifests (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`), required since 2024. Declare tracking domains and an approved reason code for each required-reason API you touch, such as user defaults, file timestamps, or disk space. Third-party SDKs on Apple's list must ship their own manifest and a code signature, so an SDK that has not caught up becomes your submission problem.

Google:
• The Data safety form in Play Console — collected, shared, retained, encrypted in transit, deletable.
• The advertising ID needs its permission declared, and it vanishes when the user opts out, so never treat it as a stable identifier.
• Apps with accounts need an in-app account deletion path and a web deletion URL.

GDPR and its relatives:
• Establish a lawful basis, and gate non-essential SDK initialisation on consent. The SDK must not start before the user answers, which means the gate belongs in the startup path, not in a screen.
• Build the user-rights endpoints for real: access, export, deletion. Deletion has to reach the device too — local database, caches, Keychain and Keystore entries.
• Watch data residency for EU and UK users; some contracts require the data never to leave the region.

Engineering practice: keep an inventory of every SDK and what it sends on first launch, and re-audit on every version bump. An SDK update is an unreviewed change to your privacy posture.
